name: Arek Borucki
bio: Arek Borucki is a Machine Learning Platform & Database Engineer at Hugging Face, where he helps keep the infrastructure behind one of the world's largest open-source AI platforms running at scale. He is the author of MongoDB in Action 8.0 and co-author of Mastering MongoDB 7.0. With over 10 years of experience in SRE, Kubernetes, AWS, GCP, and managing MongoDB in production, from 100TB+ sharded clusters to cloud-native deployments, he brings deep expertise in databases, platform engineering, and infrastructure at scale.

talks.title: Serving 2 Million Models Without Melting: Scaling the Hugging Face Hub

sessions.scheduled_title: Serving 2 Million Models Without Melting: Scaling the Hugging Face Hub

quotes.quote: Just to give you some perspective, few years ago we had 20,000 models. Today 3 million. It is around 150x increase in just last couple of years.
In 2022, we had 10K. In 2024, 100K. Less than a year ago, we had 500K. Today, 1 million.
All this data must be stored, indexed, and also must be searchable. And that's the hardest part.
At 20,000 models, any query is fast. Even without an index, trust me, no one would notice.
With 14 million users, even 1% is a not small number. It is 140,000 of people hitting slow search at scale. P99 is much more important than P50
MongoDB does not store the models themselves. It stores everything about the models.
This separation of concern let us scale metadata independently from binary storage and compute independently from both.
We tokenize model names on insert time, not at query time.
This solution was working well as long as data set was small. Reax doesn't scale well.
this solution is much more efficient and is so far scale well, so we don't have any more latency issues in our search bar.
First all queries which doesn't require the latest data goes to secondaries. Only queries that must have strong consistency stay on primary
Aggregations pipelines that scan large amount of data, sort, group or transform the data should not go on primary. They are heavy. Secondaries are better placed for them.
The pattern is simple. Primary should focus on what only primary can do. Anything else can be pushed to different machines.
The key difference between replica set cluster and sharded cluster is replica set keep full data set on each node.
There is also shard key which must be selected. This is not trivial operation but this talk is not about choosing short key.
Our deployment hub deployment can scale from 10 to 500 bots depends of on the traffic.
HPA scale only based on CPU and memory. KDA scale on real application metrics like request per second or event loop utilization.
This is what scaling medium models is really about. Keeping the user experience simple no matter how complex it gets under the hood.

positions.claim: Regex-based search in MongoDB does not scale, and full-text search on Apache Lucene (Atlas Search) is the right replacement once the dataset grows large.
P99 latency matters more than P50 for user-facing search at Hugging Face's scale.
Tokenization should happen at insert time rather than query time so autocomplete can match instantly.
Reads and listings should be served from a separate denormalized collection rather than the primary source-of-truth repo collection.
Model artifacts belong in object storage while metadata belongs in a database, so the two can scale independently.

The database primary should only handle writes and queries requiring strong consistency; everything else — heavy aggregations, change streams, ad hoc and reporting queries — should be pushed to secondaries or a hidden node.
A single MongoDB replica set will soon be insufficient for Hugging Face's growth, making sharding the necessary next step.
Choosing a shard key is a non-trivial decision.
Two-layer autoscaling (pod-level plus node-level via Cast AI) keeps the Hub healthy without manual intervention and without overprovisioning, making it cost effective.

KEDA is superior to HPA for this workload because scaling on application metrics like request rate captures load that CPU and memory thresholds miss, such as a pod with low CPU but a high request queue.
Slow search causes users to leave for alternatives, which is why search latency is treated as a first-order infrastructure priority.
Good infrastructure at this scale is invisible — success means users never think about it.
